segments.title: Introduction to Big O notation in computer science

sub_topics.name: Introduction to the topic
sub_topics.description: Hey, what's going on everybody? It's your bro, hope you're doing well, and in this video I'm going to describe the very basics of Big O notation in, well, computer science.

sub_topics.name: Big O notation definition
sub_topics.description: So sit back, relax, and enjoy the show. Oh yeah, Big O notation. So a common phrase used with Big O notation is, how code slows as data grows. It describes the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases.

key_points: Big O notation is used to describe the performance of an algorithm
It focuses on the number of steps to complete an algorithm

segments.title: Examples of Big O notation

sub_topics.name: Example of a linear time function
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument. The for loop within here will iterate once up to whatever number that n is, add i to sum, then return it.

sub_topics.name: Example of a constant time function
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum. So if n was, let's say, a million, this is still only going to take a couple seconds. steps. Three steps, not a million steps.

sub_topics.name: Constant time complexity explanation
sub_topics.description: It's going to be completed in the same amount of steps. So this function is way better than this previous one. Three steps is better than a million steps.

key_points: Constant time complexity is the best
Linear time complexity is proportional to the input size
Constant time complexity is independent of the input size

segments.title: Runtime complexities and their explanations

sub_topics.name: Introduction to runtime complexities
sub_topics.description: Here's a graph that I made to represent the different runtime complexities. We have data on the x-axis represented by n. So data will increase as we go more to the right, and we have time on the y-axis.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(1) - constant time
sub_topics.description: Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of 1 will take the same amount of time regardless of the data size. A few examples would include the random access of an element within an array and inserting at the beginning of a linked list.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(log n) - logarithmic time
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of log n, also known as logarithmic time. One example is binary search.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(n) - linear time
sub_topics.description: O is also known as linear time. As the amount of data increases, the time it takes to complete something will increase proportionally linearly.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(n log n) - quasi-linear time
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of N log N, also known as quasi-linear time. This would include a quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(n^2) - quadratic time
sub_topics.description: Then we have O of n squared, also known as quadratic time. A few examples would include insertion sort, selection sort, and bubble sort.

sub_topics.name: Comparison of linear and quadratic time
sub_topics.description: So just to compare linear time and quadratic time, with linear time if our data set was a thousand if n equals a thousand it going to take a thousand steps they proportional they linear but if we were using quadratic time if n was a thousand then a thousand squared would be a million.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of O(n!) - factorial time
sub_topics.description: And lastly, we have O of n factorial, also known as factorial time, and one place where this is used is with the traveling salesman problem, which I might discuss in a future video.

sub_topics.name: Conclusion
sub_topics.description: Well, that's the very basics of Big O notation. It's notation used to describe the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases.

key_points: Each has its own characteristics and examples
Understanding runtime complexities is crucial in computer science
